Confidence Interval for the Noncentrality Parameter of a Noncentral t Distribution

Source: R/ci_nc_t.R
ci_nc_t.Rd

Finds the noncentrality parameters of a noncentral t-distribution that bracket an observed t-value with the requested tail probabilities, giving a confidence interval on the population noncentrality parameter. Together with ci_nc_F and ci_nc_chisq, this is one of the low-level noncentral distribution workhorses on which the ci_* confidence interval functions (e.g., ci_smd, ci_smd_c, ci_cv) are built; most analyses reach it through those functions rather than calling it directly. The function corresponds to conf.limits.nct() in MBESS; its name places it in the ci_* family because a confidence interval is what it computes.

Usage

ci_nc_t(
  ncp,
  df,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  alpha_lower = NULL,
  alpha_upper = NULL,
  tol = 1e-09,
  verbose = TRUE,
  ...
)

Arguments

ncp

The observed t-value, which is the estimate of the noncentrality parameter the interval is formed for

df

The degrees of freedom

conf_level

The level of confidence for a symmetric confidence interval. A level above .999999998, whose tail areas are below 1e-9, is refused (see "Small tail areas" in Details)

alpha_lower

The proportion of values beyond the lower limit of the confidence interval (cannot be used with conf_level): 0, for an interval with no lower limit, or at least 1e-9 (see "Small tail areas" in Details)

alpha_upper

The proportion of values beyond the upper limit of the confidence interval (cannot be used with conf_level): 0, for an interval with no upper limit, or at least 1e-9

tol

The convergence tolerance passed to uniroot when locating each limit

verbose

If TRUE (the default), the returned data frame additionally reports the achieved tail probabilities at each limit; if FALSE, only term and value are returned

...

Additional arguments forwarded to uniroot

Value

A data.frame with one row per confidence limit and the columns:

term

Either "ci_lower" or "ci_upper".

value

The noncentrality parameter at that limit. -Inf when alpha_lower = 0; Inf when alpha_upper = 0.

prob_less

(verbose = TRUE) The probability \(P(T \le \mathrm{ncp})\) that a t-statistic from the noncentral t-distribution centered at the row's limit falls at or below the observed ncp. By construction this equals alpha_upper on the ci_upper row and \(1 - \mathtt{alpha\_lower}\) on the ci_lower row.

prob_greater

(verbose = TRUE) The complementary probability \(P(T \ge \mathrm{ncp})\). By construction this equals alpha_lower on the ci_lower row and \(1 - \mathtt{alpha\_upper}\) on the ci_upper row.

Details

Each confidence limit is the noncentrality parameter of a noncentral t-distribution with df degrees of freedom whose appropriate tail at the observed ncp contains the requested probability:

  • the lower limit satisfies \(P(T \ge \mathrm{ncp}) = \mathtt{alpha\_lower}\);

  • the upper limit satisfies \(P(T \le \mathrm{ncp}) = \mathtt{alpha\_upper}\).

Each tail probability is continuous and strictly monotone in the noncentrality parameter, so each limit is the unique root of a one-dimensional equation. The roots are located with uniroot starting from a bracket centered on ncp with half-width scaled by the asymptotic standard error of the noncentrality estimator; extendInt is used to widen the bracket if needed.

Computation. R's pt() sums a series for the noncentral t distribution up to a noncentrality of 37.62 and with at most 400,000 degrees of freedom, and returns a normal approximation otherwise. Compared with the exact probability over a grid of degrees of freedom, noncentralities, and quantiles (from \(10^{-6}\) to \(1 - 10^{-6}\)), it was within \(10^{-9}\) up to a noncentrality of 37.62 with at most 2,000 degrees of freedom and up to 33 with more (the series stops short in the upper tail near the top of its range: the error was \(10^{-6}\) at 34 and .001 at 36 with 100,000 degrees of freedom), while the normal approximation was off by as much as .14 with one degree of freedom, .008 with 38, and .001 with 1,000; below one degree of freedom it is not accurate at any noncentrality other than 0. Each limit is therefore found with pt() where the limit lies in that range (with at least one degree of freedom), and otherwise with the exact probability $$P(T \le t) = \int_0^\infty \Phi(t s - \lambda)\, f(s)\, ds,$$ where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function, \(f\) the density of \(S = \sqrt{V/\nu}\) for \(V\) chi square on \(\nu\) degrees of freedom, and \(T = (Z + \lambda)/S\) with \(Z\) standard normal, independent of \(V\); the integral is computed numerically. The limits agreed with bisection on a second exact form, which conditions on the normal variate instead, to within \(3.5 \times 10^{-9}\) of the width of the interval in 400 random cases with 1 to 1,000,000 degrees of freedom. The tail probabilities in prob_less and prob_greater are computed the same way as the limit in their row. A limit outside the range takes about a millisecond; one inside it, a tenth of that.

Small tail areas. A nonzero tail area below 1e-9, or a conf_level above .999999998, is refused with an error of class dmar_argument_invalid whose reason is "tail_below_floor". A limit is the root of a tail probability, and pt() sums its series to an absolute tolerance of \(10^{-12}\) and forms one tail as 1 minus the other, so the error of the probability becomes a larger part of the tail as the tail shrinks. Against the exact probability, the limits with equal tails at \(t\) = 5 on 47 degrees of freedom, .5 on 10, 2 on 200, 10 on 20, -3 on 30, and 1 on 1,000, at 66 tail areas from \(10^{-6}\) down to \(10^{-9}\), were off by at most \(1.7 \times 10^{-5}\) at tail areas of \(10^{-8}\) and above, \(7.3 \times 10^{-5}\) at \(2 \times 10^{-9}\) and above, and \(1.4 \times 10^{-4}\) at \(10^{-9}\) (the upper limit at \(t\) = 10 on 20 degrees of freedom, \(6.0 \times 10^{-6}\) of the width of the interval); at \(10^{-10}\) the largest error was \(1.1 \times 10^{-3}\), and at \(10^{-20}\) the upper limit at \(t\) = 5 on 47 degrees of freedom was 7.6 percent too small. Every interval and plan whose limits come from this function keeps the floor, among them ci_smd, ci_smd_c, ci_sm, ci_cv, ci_sc, ci_sc_ancova, ci_src, and ci_reg_coef with noncentral = TRUE, and the planners of those intervals. The central intervals of a contrast, a correlation, and a regression coefficient (ci_c, ci_r, ci_rc, and ci_reg_coef with noncentral = FALSE) and their planners (ss_aipe_c, ss_aipe_r, and ss_aipe_rc) keep it too, so that an interval and the plan for it accept the same tail areas.

A limit past 37.62. Each limit is found by its own rule, so an interval can have its lower limit from pt() and its upper limit from the exact probability. The interval for the standardized mean difference of two groups of 20 at \(d = 10\) with 99 percent confidence (ci_smd) is such an interval: it is [7.003, 13.099], 6.096 wide. In 100,000 samples of two groups of 20 with \(\delta = 13\), this 99 percent interval fell below \(\delta\) in .52 percent and above it in .48 percent (.50 percent each by design).

This function is especially useful for forming confidence intervals around standardized mean differences (Cohen's d, Glass's g, Hedges' g), standardized regression coefficients, and coefficients of variation.

References

Cumming, G., & Finch, S. (2001). A primer on the understanding, use, and calculation of confidence intervals that are based on central and noncentral distributions. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 61(4), 532–574. doi:10.1177/0013164401614002

Kelley, K. (2005). The effects of nonnormal distributions on confidence intervals around the standardized mean difference: Bootstrap and parametric confidence intervals, Educational and Psychological Measurement, 65, 51–69. doi:10.1177/0013164404264850

Kelley, K. (2007). Confidence intervals for standardized effect sizes: Theory, application, and implementation. Journal of Statistical Software, 20(8), 1–24. doi:10.18637/jss.v020.i08

Steiger, J. H., & Fouladi, R. T. (1997). Noncentrality interval estimation and the evaluation of statistical models. In L. L. Harlow, S. A. Mulaik, & J. H. Steiger (Eds.), What if there were no significance tests? (pp. 221–257). Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum.

See also

stats::pt(), stats::qt(), uniroot, ci_smd, ci_smd_c, ci_nc_F, ci_nc_chisq

Other noncentral distribution confidence intervals: ci_nc_F(), ci_nc_chisq()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# Suppose observed t-value based on 'df'=126 is 2.83. Finding the lower
# and upper critical values for the population noncentrality parameter
# with a symmetric confidence interval with 95\% confidence is given as:
ci_nc_t(ncp = 2.83, df = 126, conf_level = .95)
#>       term     value prob_less prob_greater
#> 1 ci_lower 0.8337503     0.975        0.025
#> 2 ci_upper 4.8153591     0.025        0.975

# Modifying the above example so that a nonsymmetric 95% confidence interval
# can be formed:
ci_nc_t(ncp = 2.83, df = 126, alpha_lower = .01, alpha_upper = .04, conf_level = NULL)
#>       term    value prob_less prob_greater
#> 1 ci_lower 0.461692      0.99         0.01
#> 2 ci_upper 4.602743      0.04         0.96

# Modifying the above example so that a single-sided 95% confidence interval
# can be formed:
ci_nc_t(ncp = 2.83, df = 126, alpha_lower = 0, alpha_upper = .05, conf_level = NULL)
#>       term    value prob_less prob_greater
#> 1 ci_lower     -Inf      1.00         0.00
#> 2 ci_upper 4.495225      0.05         0.95
